title: Is A Water Infection The Same As A UTI?
h1: Is A Water Infection The Same As A UTI?
description: General information about urinary symptoms that people sometimes call a water infection or a wee infection, and when a general practice appointment may help.
headings: When Should I Seek Medical Advice?
keywords: knowledge articles is a water infection the same as a uti
text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Symptoms & Everyday Concerns Is A Water Infection The Same As A UTI? A person with burning, needing to pass urine more often, or what they call a water infection often wants to know whether a GP appointment is the right next step. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-19 Introduction A change in how it feels to pass urine raises a practical question: is this a water infection, and what do I ask for? This guide explains those everyday words for men and women. It does not diagnose a cause and it does not describe treatment. What Is It? People use water infection, wee infection, and UTI for a change in how it feels to pass urine. Those phrases point to the same kind of concern. They are not a diagnosis. Stinging as urine is passed Needing to pass urine more often than usual A new urge that is hard to put off This guide is not a prostate check. A prostate guide is a different topic. Should I Be Concerned? A new change in how it feels to pass urine is an everyday reason a general practice visit can help, including when water infection or UTI is the wording you are using. The same threshold applies for men and women. This guide does not judge how serious a symptom is. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Seek medical advice when you would otherwise guess the cause, or when the symptoms are worsening. Do not use this page to decide that they can wait. Urgent care. If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening, or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. Do not use the booking form for emergency care. How Can a GP Help? A general practitioner can listen to what has changed and decide whether an examination or a follow-up plan is appropriate. That assessment happens at a general practice visit. This guide does not name a practitioner and it does not describe a procedure. Ask reception for a general practice appointment and say what has changed. This page does not choose an appointment type. If you are unsure which appointment to book, call reception on (07) 3217 3344. Men and women can both book a general practice visit. Frequently Asked Questions Is a bladder infection the same words? Bladder infection is another phrase people use for this same concern. Saying it does not tell you the cause. Does this mean I need a prostate check? No. Needing to pass urine more often does not turn this page into a prostate check. That question stays in a men's health guide. title: What Is Preventive Care?
description: Learn how preventive healthcare uses screening, risk reviews and personalised GP advice to support long-term wellbeing.

text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Preventive Healthcare What Is Preventive Healthcare? Understand preventive healthcare, how screening and risk assessment work and why prevention should be personalised rather than based on a generic checklist. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Preventive healthcare aims to reduce avoidable illness, identify important risks early and help people stay well for longer. It includes screening and vaccination, but also involves reviewing lifestyle, family history and risks that may change over time. Why This Topic Matters Preventive healthcare aims to reduce illness and identify risks early. It is tailored to a person’s age, family history and circumstances; doing more tests does not always mean better care. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Opportunities include checking blood pressure, discussing cardiovascular risk, reviewing vaccination status, and considering cancer screening invitations. New symptoms need diagnostic review, not only a preventive check. You want help deciding which tests are actually useful. Your family history or health risks have changed. You have missed screening or immunisation milestones. Prevention is planned care before problems become urgent Examples include blood pressure checks, recommended cancer screening, vaccination, cardiovascular and diabetes risk assessment, smoking cessation and support with nutrition, physical activity, sleep and mental wellbeing. Good preventive care is selective. Tests and screening should have a clear evidence-based purpose, because more testing is not automatically better and can sometimes lead to unnecessary follow-up. Use national screening programs where eligible Review vaccination according to age and risk Discuss family history and changing risk factors Build prevention into an ongoing GP relationship When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Consider a preventive appointment if you are unsure what screening is due, have not reviewed your health risks for some time or your family, medical or lifestyle circumstances have changed. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can review your personal risks, identify appropriate screening and vaccination, discuss realistic risk reduction and create a plan for follow-up rather than treating prevention as a one-off event. Preventive care can be built into routine GP visits for patients across Woolloongabba and Brisbane's inner south rather than treated as a one-off checklist. Frequently Asked Questions Is preventive healthcare only screening? No. It also includes vaccination, risk-factor management, lifestyle support and monitoring of emerging health risks. Do I need every test every year? No. Testing should be based on age, risk, symptoms, previous results and current clinical guidance. Can prevention be part of normal GP care? Yes. Routine appointments can identify preventive needs, with a separate longer review arranged when more time is useful. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction A health assessment is a structured review of health risks and preventive needs. It is not the same as ordering a broad set of tests. The content depends on the reason for the assessment, your age, medical history and any specific Medicare eligibility criteria. Why This Topic Matters A health assessment is a structured review of selected health needs, function and risks. Specific Medicare-funded assessments have eligibility rules and are not universal annual checks. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Topics can include mobility, falls, medicines, living arrangements, memory, chronic conditions and screening history. The appointment may lead to advice, follow-up or referral based on identified needs. You want to know whether you qualify for a particular health assessment. You or a family member notice changes in independence or safety. Multiple health issues would benefit from a coordinated plan. A useful health assessment connects history, examination and prevention A GP may review current conditions, medicines, blood pressure, lifestyle, vaccination, screening, mobility, mental wellbeing and other risks relevant to the assessment. Tests are then selected when there is a clinical reason. Some Medicare-funded health assessments are available only to particular age or risk groups and have specific requirements. Eligibility should be checked against current Medicare rules rather than assumed. Bring a current medicines list Know your family history where possible Bring recent reports if they are not already available to the practice Ask what follow-up will occur if a risk is identified When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a preventive review if you have received an invitation, think you may qualify for a specific assessment or simply need a broader review of health risks. New symptoms should still be assessed on their own merits. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can determine what type of assessment is relevant, review risks in context, arrange targeted testing, update preventive care and document a follow-up plan. Preventive care can be built into routine GP visits for patients across Woolloongabba and Brisbane's inner south rather than treated as a one-off checklist. Frequently Asked Questions Is a health assessment just a blood test? No. It is a broader clinical review. Blood tests may be included when relevant but are not the entire assessment. Are all health assessments covered by Medicare? No. Medicare-funded assessment items have eligibility and timing rules. Reception and your GP can confirm what applies. Preventive care should focus on maintaining function and independence while managing conditions, medicines and screening in a way that matches your goals. Why This Topic Matters Good health in later life includes independence, relationships and everyday function. Preventing falls, maintaining strength, protecting bone health and reviewing medicines can be as important as screening tests. Healthy ageing combines prevention with day-to-day function Regular review may include blood pressure, vaccination, cancer screening, medicines, nutrition, activity, strength and balance, hearing, vision, sleep, mood, memory and chronic conditions. Preventive priorities can also change after a hospital admission, fall, new diagnosis or major medicine change. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Skin Health & Skin Cancer Why Skin Checks Matter In Australia Why skin awareness and risk-based skin checks matter in Australia, what to watch for and how a GP can assess concerning spots. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Australia has high ultraviolet exposure and a high burden of skin cancer. Skin awareness matters because many skin cancers are first noticed as a new spot or a change to an existing one. A skin check is an opportunity to assess concerning lesions and individual risk. Why This Topic Matters Australia has substantial ultraviolet exposure, and skin cancer is common. Skin examinations focus on concerning lesions and personal risk; a GP can advise whether regular checks are suitable for you. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Watch for changing moles, new spots, sores that do not heal or lesions that bleed without explanation. Skin type, sunburn history and previous skin cancers influence the appropriate assessment plan. A mole is changing in size, shape or colour. A spot bleeds, crusts or repeatedly fails to heal. You have previous skin cancer or substantial risk and need an individual monitoring plan. Early attention to change is more useful than waiting for symptoms Skin cancers do not all look the same. Changes in size, shape, colour or texture, a spot that looks different from others, a sore that does not heal, bleeding or persistent tenderness can all justify medical review. There is no single skin-check interval that is right for everyone. Personal risk depends on factors such as previous skin cancer, sun exposure, skin type, number and type of moles, family history and immune status. Become familiar with your own skin Check areas that are hard to see as well as sun-exposed skin Book promptly for a new or changing lesion Discuss your personal risk rather than relying on a generic interval When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book a medical assessment for a new, changing, bleeding, non-healing or otherwise concerning spot. Rapidly changing lesions or symptoms that concern you should not be delayed until a routine future check. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can examine the skin, use dermoscopy where available and appropriate, decide whether monitoring, biopsy, treatment or specialist referral is needed, and discuss a risk-based approach to future checks. For patients living and working around Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and Greenslopes, sun protection and skin awareness are relevant throughout much of the year. Frequently Asked Questions How often should I have a skin check? The appropriate interval depends on your individual risk and history. Ask your clinician what is reasonable for you. Can skin cancer occur on areas that are not usually in the sun? Yes. Although UV exposure is a major risk, skin cancers can appear in less exposed areas, so whole-skin awareness is important. What if a mole looks different from my other moles? A spot that looks or behaves differently from others is worth medical assessment, especially if it is new or changing. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Skin Health & Skin Cancer Understanding Skin Cancer Risks Understand major skin cancer risk factors in Australia and how personal risk can guide prevention and medical review. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction Ultraviolet radiation is the main preventable cause of skin cancer, but individual risk is also shaped by skin type, age, previous skin cancers, family history, immune suppression and patterns of sun exposure over time. Why This Topic Matters Ultraviolet radiation is a major preventable skin cancer risk. Family history, earlier skin cancers, fair skin and cumulative sun exposure may increase personal risk, but people of every skin tone can develop skin cancer. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise The appearance of skin cancer varies. A new or evolving spot, irregular pigmentation, persistent scaly patch or non-healing sore deserves attention rather than reliance on a single visual checklist. You have a previous melanoma or another skin cancer. You have an evolving or suspicious lesion. You want to discuss sun protection and a risk-based skin examination plan. Risk accumulates, and it is not limited to obvious sunburn UV damage can occur even when the weather feels mild or cloudy. Repeated exposure over many years matters, and a history of intense intermittent exposure or previous skin cancer can increase future risk. People with darker skin can also develop skin cancer. Risk may be lower for some types, but new or changing lesions should still be assessed rather than dismissed because of skin tone. Previous skin cancer increases future risk Fair skin and a tendency to burn can increase UV vulnerability Family history and large numbers of atypical moles may matter Immune suppression can increase risk Protection is important whenever UV levels require it When Should I Seek Medical Advice? See a clinician for any new, changing, bleeding or non-healing lesion, or if you have a high-risk history and are unsure how often your skin should be reviewed. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can take a personal risk history, examine lesions, advise on prevention and determine whether biopsy, treatment, monitoring or specialist referral is appropriate. For patients living and working around Woolloongabba, South Brisbane and Greenslopes, sun protection and skin awareness are relevant throughout much of the year. Frequently Asked Questions Is sunburn the only way UV causes damage? No. UV damage can accumulate without obvious sunburn and can occur even on cooler or cloudy days. Does darker skin eliminate skin cancer risk? No. Darker skin can provide more natural protection from UV, but skin cancer can still occur. Does having one skin cancer change future risk? Yes. A previous skin cancer is an important risk factor and may change how often follow-up is recommended. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Skin Health & Skin Cancer When Should I Book A Skin Check? Know when a new or changing skin spot should be assessed and how a risk-based skin check differs from a fixed annual rule. Patient education Australian primary-care context Updated 2026-10-08 Introduction You do not need to wait for a scheduled annual check if you notice a concerning skin change. New or changing lesions, non-healing sores and spots that look different from the rest are reasons to seek assessment earlier. Why This Topic Matters You do not need to wait for a scheduled yearly review when a lesion changes. Risk-based skin examinations and the assessment of a specific suspicious spot are different conversations. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Bring information about when the mark appeared, any changes, past skin pathology and family history. Photos with dates can help describe a change but cannot replace an in-person examination. A new spot is visibly changing. A lesion is painful, bleeding, persistent or not healing. You have a personal or strong family history of skin cancer. Book because of change or risk, not only because a year has passed A full skin review may be useful for people with significant sun exposure, previous skin cancer, many unusual moles, immune suppression or other important risk factors. Other people may be advised to self-monitor and seek review when something changes. During an appointment, the clinician may inspect the skin and use a dermatoscope to look more closely at particular spots. A suspicious lesion may need photography, planned review, biopsy, treatment or referral. New spot that continues to change Existing spot changing in colour, shape, size or texture Sore that does not heal Lesion that repeatedly bleeds, crusts, itches or becomes tender High-risk personal history that needs planned surveillance When Should I Seek Medical Advice? If a spot is changing quickly or bleeding repeatedly, do not wait for a distant routine appointment simply because you have a future skin check booked. Urgent care: If symptoms are severe, rapidly worsening or you believe there is a life-threatening emergency, call 000. How Can a GP Help? A GP can assess the lesion and the rest of your risk profile, determine whether further investigation is needed and recommend an appropriate future surveillance interval. Protection is important when UV levels are high enough to damage unprotected skin. Why This Topic Matters In Queensland, UV exposure can be high even when the weather feels mild. Protection is recommended whenever the UV index is 3 or higher; the goal is to reduce cumulative exposure, not avoid outdoor activity altogether. Signs, Symptoms or Situations to Recognise Choose shade, protective clothing, a broad-brimmed hat, sunglasses and suitable sunscreen applied according to the label. Sunscreen should complement, not replace, clothing and shade. Check the daily UV level and plan outdoor activity around it when possible. Reapply sunscreen according to current guidance, especially after swimming, heavy sweating or towel drying. Cover skin with protective clothing Use broad-spectrum water-resistant SPF50 or SPF50+ sunscreen Wear a broad-brimmed hat and sunglasses Seek shade Check your skin regularly for new or changing spots When Should I Seek Medical Advice? text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Telehealth & Access To Care When Can I Use Telehealth? Find out when GP telehealth may be suitable, when in-person examination is necessary and what Medicare eligibility questions to ask. Introduction Telehealth allows some GP consultations by telephone or video without travelling to the practice. It can be convenient for selected follow-ups, care discussions and results, but it is not appropriate for every concern. Your safety and the need for an examination guide the choice. Why This Topic Matters A conversation alone cannot replace measurements, examination or a procedure when these are clinically needed. Medicare-rebated GP telehealth also has specific eligibility requirements, including an established patient relationship in many circumstances and exemptions for some groups and services. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: A planned follow-up or discussion that may not require physical examination. Questions about medicines or existing results where your clinician agrees telehealth is suitable. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Vaccinations Influenza Vaccination: Who Should Consider It? Learn who should consider annual influenza vaccination in Australia, who may receive funded vaccines and when to ask your GP. Introduction Influenza is a viral respiratory infection that can be more severe than the common cold. Vaccination is an important way to reduce the risk of influenza illness and complications. Australian recommendations and available formulations are reviewed each season. Why This Topic Matters The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends influenza vaccination each year for everyone aged six months and older. National Immunisation Program funding is available for certain eligible groups; the vaccine and dose schedule depend on age, medical history and current advice. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: You are pregnant, aged 65 or older, caring for a young child, or have a chronic condition that increases influenza risk. Your child is at least six months old and has not had the current season's recommended dose or doses. You have not reviewed eligibility for funded vaccination or the available seasonal formulation. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Arrange a vaccination discussion before the main influenza season where practical, but vaccination can still be useful later. If you are acutely unwell, ask whether to defer. Seek urgent care for severe breathing difficulty, confusion or other concerning illness; a vaccine appointment is not treatment for an emergency. How Can a GP Help? A GP or appropriately qualified immunisation provider can review your age, pregnancy, risk conditions and vaccination history to advise on the right seasonal vaccine. Some first-time vaccinations in young children or certain higher-risk groups require extra doses under current guidance. Confirm availability with the clinic. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions Does everyone need a flu vaccination every year? Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for people aged six months and older; the suitable product and funding vary. Is the influenza vaccination free for everyone? No. The National Immunisation Program funds vaccines for eligible groups; charges and consultation arrangements should be checked. Can I have a flu vaccine when pregnant? Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy. Ask your clinician about the appropriate non-live vaccine. text: Healthcare Knowledge Centre · Vaccinations Travel Vaccinations Before Overseas Travel Planning overseas travel? Learn why travel vaccination advice depends on destination, itinerary and health history. Introduction Travel health preparation depends on where you are going, how long you will stay and what you plan to do. A short city break, rural volunteering trip and extended family visit can involve different infectious disease risks even in the same country. Why This Topic Matters Some vaccines need multiple doses or time to provide protection. Travel advice may also cover food and water safety, mosquito-borne disease, malaria prevention, medication supplies and medical access while overseas. Routine Australian vaccinations should be checked as well. Signs, Symptoms or Situations Relevant to Patients The following situations are worth recognising. They do not establish a diagnosis by themselves: You are travelling to regions where hepatitis A, typhoid, yellow fever or other infections may be relevant. Your trip includes remote travel, animal contact, long stays or visiting friends and relatives. You have chronic disease, pregnancy, immune suppression or a complex medicine history. When Should I Seek Medical Advice? Book travel advice well before departure—ideally at least six to eight weeks in advance where possible. Seek guidance sooner if departure is near; some protective steps may still be available. A fever during or after travel, especially after visiting a malaria-risk area, needs prompt medical assessment. How Can a GP Help? Your GP can review routine immunisations, destination-specific guidance and whether specialist travel vaccination services are needed. Bring your itinerary and vaccine record. Some vaccines have specific certification or provider requirements, so availability and any need for referral should be confirmed rather than assumed. Patients from Woolloongabba and nearby Brisbane inner-south communities can discuss the most appropriate next step with the practice. Frequently Asked Questions How early should I book travel advice? Several weeks before departure is preferable, often six to eight, because some vaccine courses need time. Are travel vaccines the same for every country? No. Recommendations depend on destination, season, accommodation, activity, individual health and previous vaccination. Can my GP provide every travel vaccine? Not necessarily. Certain vaccines require accredited providers; your GP can advise on referral and availability.
